points: Possible prodrome: malaise, headache, sore throat, low-grade fever (URTI — Case 3).
**Herald patch:** single, 2–5 cm, oval, salmon-pink (grey-brown/violaceous in darker skin) plaque with fine **collarette scale** inside the edge; often trunk, upper arm, neck, thigh.
Variants: **inverse** (flexural — axillae/groin, commoner in children/skin of colour), papular, vesicular, purpuric, urticarial, giant, unilateral, oral lesions.
Darker skin: more papular/facial lesions; prolonged post-inflammatory hyper/hypopigmentation.
(treponemal EIA ± RPR) if atypical, palms/soles involved, no herald patch, sexual risk, or lasting >12 weeks.
if the herald patch alone looks like tinea (scale at advancing edge).

cards.name: Guttate psoriasis
cards.clue: Many small (0.5–1 cm) **drop-like papules** with thicker **silvery scale** over the whole lesion, **no herald patch**, 1–3 weeks after **streptococcal sore throat**/tonsillitis; may have family history, nail pitting, scalp involvement; can persist/evolve into plaque psoriasis

cards.name: Secondary syphilis
cards.clue: **Palms and soles** copper-red papules, mucous patches, condylomata lata, patchy alopecia, generalised lymphadenopathy, malaise; papules **tender to blunt pressure (Buschke–Ollendorff sign)**; sexual history; positive serology

cards.name: Tinea corporis (vs herald patch)
cards.clue: Annular, active scaly edge with central clearing, scale at advancing edge, often asymmetric; KOH/scraping positive

cards.name: Nummular (discoid) eczema
cards.clue: Coin-shaped, very itchy, crusted/oozing, limbs > trunk

cards.name: Pityriasiform drug eruption
cards.clue: New drug, larger lesions, no herald patch, persists, eosinophils on biopsy

cards.name: Pityriasis versicolor
cards.clue: Fine scale, hypo/hyperpigmented, upper trunk, Malassezia on scraping, chronic

cards.name: Pityriasis lichenoides chronica
cards.clue: Small red-brown papules with mica-like scale, recurrent crops over months

points: Explain benign, **non-contagious**, self-limiting (6–12 weeks); no isolation needed; scars do not occur (pigment change may persist months in darker skin).
Emollients and soap substitutes; avoid hot showers, perfumed products, tight clothes; moderate sun exposure may speed resolution in some.
**Pregnancy:** PR in pregnancy (esp. first 15 weeks) has been associated with miscarriage/premature delivery — inform/refer to midwife/obstetrician (CKS).
Atypical features, palms/soles/mucosal involvement or sexual risk → **syphilis serology / refer to sexual health (GUM)**.
Persisting >12 weeks, diagnostic doubt, severe symptoms → GP/dermatology.
Suspected drug cause → review medication with prescriber.

items.t: Palm or sole lesions, mouth ulcers, lymphadenopathy or sexual risk: **syphilis serology** and sexual-health referral.
Pityriasis rosea in the **first 15 weeks of pregnancy**: inform the midwife or obstetric team.
Lasting more than 3 months: reconsider the diagnosis.

pearls.t: "One big patch first, then many small ovals along the ribs" = PR; "shower of small drops after strep throat" = guttate psoriasis.
The herald patch is often mis-treated as ringworm — antifungal failure is a clue.
**Every generalised papulosquamous rash: ask about sexual history and look at palms and soles.**
Do not prescribe oral steroids for PR (may prolong/worsen).
Provide BAD/PCDS patient leaflet; review if not resolving by 3 months.
